name: VMT19937 (V-family and X-family vectorized Mersenne Twister)
baseline: std::mt19937_64 (the 'STL-MT19937-64' rows); also the original reference MT19937 / SFMT19937 and Intel MKL MT/SFMT
workload: Throughput in million samples/s of 32-bit (MT19937, SFMT19937) and 64-bit (MT19937-64) random numbers, about 1.6e10 numbers per CPU (30 runs of 8.19e6 samples), in scalar (one value per call) and vectorial (block of 10,240) query modes, on five CPU targets (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, SVE256).
claimed_speedup: README table, M samples/s, vectorial mode: V-MT19937-64 2865 (AVX-512) / 1161 (AVX2) vs STL-MT19937-64 590 / 317 (about 4.9x and 3.7x, derived from page data); V-MT19937 2392 (AVX2) vs ORIG-MT19937 259 (about 9.2x, derived from page data); V-SFMT19937 10943 (AVX-512) vs ORIG-SFMT19937 4445 (about 2.5x, derived from page data). Scalar mode: X-MT19937-64 1095 (AVX-512) vs STL 590 (about 1.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16 per doc/main.tex; Makefile default is -O3 -std=c++20 with -march=native on x86 (-march=armv8-a+simd on NEON, -march=armv8-a+sve -msve-vector-bits=256 on SVE); the bench harness is perf.exe built by the repo Makefile.
hardware: Intel Celeron J4125 2.0 GHz (SSE4.2), Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 2.3 GHz (AVX2), Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C 2.9 GHz (AVX-512), Neoverse-N1 2.5 GHz (NEON), Neoverse-V1 2.6 GHz (SVE256) (from doc/main.tex).
tradeoffs: The V-family changes the output sequence: it interleaves several MT19937 states de-phased by polynomial jump-ahead, and the sequence depends on the chosen register width (VRegBitLen). The X-family is bit-identical to the original MT19937/MT19937-64/SFMT sequences. Needs jump-polynomial data files (dat/poly) for the V-family, C++20, and SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 or NEON/SVE hardware for the large gains. Large block-fill API (block of 16 or state-size blocks) is where the speedup is.
caveats: Big speedups are in vectorial (block fill) mode; scalar single-value V-MT19937 is only about 1.7-2.1x the original reference. Intel MKL-MT is faster than V-MT19937 at AVX-512 vectorial (6479 vs 5742 M/s). The STL row exists only in the MT19937-64 table, so 32-bit std::mt19937 is not measured directly (the ORIG-MT19937 reference is the baseline there); on SVE256 STL-MT19937-64 (573) beats V-MT19937-64 scalar (513). Which standard library built the STL rows is not stated. First-party results from a single author; paper arXiv 2309.16682 could not be opened (egress blocked). CPU models and 'GCC 16' were read from the LaTeX source doc/main.tex, not the README. All ratios are derived from page data.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github VMT19937 SIMD-friendly Mersenne Twister vectorized implementation AVX-512 code'; opened the repo page, README.md, BUILD.txt, Makefile and doc/main.tex.

name: SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers, SFMT19937-64 (with SIMD) vs MT19937-64, measured by a third party (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018) in the README of sharase/melg-64.
claimed_speedup: Intel Core i7-3770: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s per 1e9 numbers (about 2.8x, derived from page data); AMD Phenom II X6 1045T: 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s (about 2.3x, derived from page data). SFMT19937-64 without SIMD: 4.2654 s and 5.6123 s (about 1.2x on both, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (stated in the melg-64 README)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40 GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70 GHz
stars_or_usage: 96 stars; widely used reference generator (also dSFMT for doubles in the same org)
tradeoffs: Produces a different sequence from MT19937, so it is not a drop-in for std::mt19937 output. Designed for 32-bit output; for 64-bit output the high-dimensional equidistribution is worse (Harase's table gives Delta=14095 vs 0 for MELG), and dSFMT is the variant meant for doubles. 128-bit SIMD blocks with SSE2, AVX2/AVX512 (added in 1.5.2), NEON (1.5.3) and Altivec backends; README warns big-endian and Altivec are not tested. C API with the state in a struct.
caveats: The SFMT repo README has no numbers; the authors' 'about twice as fast as MT19937' claim and the MCQMC 2006 paper live on pages that could not be opened (egress blocked), so this entry rests on a third-party table from the melg-64 README, measured on 2012-era CPUs with an older gcc. The baseline is the original mt19937-64.c, not libstdc++ std::mt19937_64. I did not verify that the timing harness is in the melg-64 repo.
found_via: WebSearch: 'SFMT SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister github MersenneTwister-Lab'; opened the SFMT repo page, README.txt, LICENSE.txt and commits page; the timing table is from the sharase/melg-64 README (found via github.com/topics/prng?l=c&o=desc&s=stars).

name: MELG-64 (maximally equidistributed Mersenne-prime-period generators)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers; MELG19937-64 vs MT19937-64, MT19937-64 (ID3) and SFMT19937-64 (with and without SIMD).
claimed_speedup: Intel Core i7-3770: MELG19937-64 4.2123 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s (about 1.21x, derived from page data); AMD Phenom II X6 1045T: 6.2920 s vs 6.6490 s (about 1.06x, derived from page data). README calls it 'speeds equivalent to 64-bit Mersenne Twisters'; its main point is Delta=0 (maximally equidistributed) vs 7820 for MT19937-64.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (stated in the README; build line 'gcc melg19937-64.c -o melg19937-64 -O3 -Wall')
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40 GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70 GHz
stars_or_usage: 15 stars; ACM TOMS 2018 paper (Harase and Kimoto) cited in the README
tradeoffs: 312-word state like MT19937-64, periods 2^607-1 to 2^44497-1, jump-ahead (default 2^256). Different sequence from std::mt19937_64, so not a drop-in. C code with init_by_array64 seeding.
caveats: The speed gain over MT19937-64 is modest (about 6-21%) and SFMT19937-64 with SIMD is much faster (1.8457 s and 2.8806 s); the value is equidistribution quality, not raw speed. Peer-reviewed paper cited but not opened; whether the timing harness is in the repo was not verified. 2012-era CPUs.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng?l=c&o=desc&s=stars (melg-64 listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: RANLUX++ (ranluxpp, LCG-based RANLUX reimplementation)
baseline: GCC C++ RANLUX (std::ranlux family implementation in libstdc++, 198 clock/float)
workload: Clock cycles per generated float for RANLUX-equivalent streams: the 576-bit modular-multiplication LCG form and an optimized conventional subtract-with-borrow RANLUX (scalar, SSE2, AVX2).
claimed_speedup: README: 20 clock/float for ranluxpp (Skylake) vs 198 clock/float for the GCC C++ RANLUX implementation (Haswell), 'order of magnitude faster' (about 10x, derived from page data); the optimized conventional RANLUX runs 40 clock/float scalar, SSE2 about 4x and AVX2 about 8x faster than that scalar version.
compiler_and_flags: GCC with function multiversioning (flags not stated in the README; Makefile in repo)
hardware: Skylake CPU for ranluxpp and Haswell CPU for the GCC RANLUX baseline (models not stated)
license: LGPL-3.0 (COPYING.LESSER; GPL-3.0 COPYING also in the repo)
stars_or_usage: 11 stars; a portable C version exists as jirka-h/ranluxpp-portable (0 stars, no cross-generator numbers)
tradeoffs: Reproduces the RANLUX sequences (with luxury levels) rather than a new sequence. The fast LCG path needs AMD64 assembly (mulx and adcx/adox variants) and GCC multiversioning; no portable fast path in this repo. Library files, tests/std_random_test.cxx benchmarks the standard generators.
caveats: First-party README numbers; the ranluxpp and GCC figures come from different CPU generations (Skylake vs Haswell), so the ratio is not same-machine. std::ranlux48/ranlux24 are not in the target baseline list and are slow high-quality generators, so beating them says little about beating mt19937, PCG or xoshiro. A peer-reviewed paper on the algorithm (arXiv 1705.03123) appeared in search results but was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github RANLUX++ ranluxpp Sibidanov faster than ranlux48 C++'; opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: OpenRAND (Philox, Threefry, Squares, Tyche counter-based generators)
baseline: std::mt19937 (libstdc++) on CPU and NVIDIA cuRAND on GPU
workload: Raw generation speed of the four OpenRAND generators on CPU (Google Benchmark, 10 to 100000 draws per generator instance) and GPU (GB/s of 32-bit integers produced into 1 GB), plus Brownian-walk style simulations in the paper.
claimed_speedup: README: 'as fast and often faster than native libraries like libstdc++ or Nvidia's Curand, with minimal memory overhead'; no numbers on the page. The repo benchmarks/raw_speed_cpu.cpp includes std::mt19937 as the CPU baseline.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17, works on CPU and GPU (CUDA) device code; counter-based design needs a (seed, counter) pair per work unit and gives reproducibility independent of thread count; the std-compatible engine interface lets it drive standard distributions.
caveats: The numbers (a 1.8x gain over cuRAND in a Brownian-walk test, per search results) are in the SoftwareX paper, which could not be opened, so only a qualitative first-party claim is recorded; a verifier with paper access may be able to raise the tier. The CUDA benchmark in the repo only times OpenRAND generators, so the cuRAND comparison lives in the paper. Compiler, flags and hardware are not stated on the opened pages.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github OpenRAND counter-based random number generation library Philox Tyche Squares CUDA C++ performance vs curand'; opened the repo page, README.md, benchmarks/raw_speed_cpu.cpp, benchmarks/raw_speed_cuda.cu and commits page.

name: EigenRand (vectorized random engines and distributions for Eigen)
baseline: std::mt19937_64 with the C++ <random> distributions (std::normal_distribution, std::cauchy_distribution and so on) and Eigen::DenseBase::Random; SciPy for multivariate distributions
workload: Relative speed-up of EigenRand's vectorized distributions (uniform, normal, exponential, gamma, poisson, etc.) when filling Eigen arrays, against the equivalent C++ std function or Eigen Random, on three platforms.
claimed_speedup: README: 'You can get 5~10 times speed by just replacing old Eigen's Random or unvectorizable c++11 random number generators with EigenRand'; the per-distribution speed-up values are in chart images and on the repo's GitHub Actions release workflow page (cells in orange are slower than the reference).
compiler_and_flags: Windows 2019 MSVC 19.29.30147; Ubuntu 18.04 GCC 7.5.0; macOS Monterey 12.2.1 clang 13.1.6; Eigen 3.4.0; target machine options such as -mavx2 are user-supplied (flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8171M (AVX2); Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C (AVX2); Apple M1 Pro (NEON)
tradeoffs: Requires Eigen (3.3.4 to 3.4.0 or 5.0.x). Vectorized math functions can lose precision (the README reports a distribution-fit table). Ships a vectorized mt19937_64 (Vmt19937_64, sequence depends on SIMD width) and P8_mt19937_64 (eight streams, same values on every architecture). Output values differ from the std distributions.
caveats: Speed-ups are only in chart images and on a CI page, not in README text, and the baseline for several distributions is a non-vectorized std function or Eigen's rand()-based Random, so the comparison is against weak baselines; some distributions are slower than their references. Compilers are old (GCC 7.5, MSVC 19.29).
found_via: WebSearch: 'github alias method discrete distribution C++ faster than std::discrete_distribution benchmark' (EigenRand listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: normaldist-benchmark (Box-Muller SSE2/AVX and Ziggurat normal generators)
workload: Time per sample (ns) to generate 1 million standard-normal samples (min of 10 trials) in single and double precision; each algorithm is in its own file and all but cpp11random use a simple LCG as the uniform source.
claimed_speedup: normaldistf (float): cpp11random 18.642 ns vs boxmuller_avx 2.253 ns (about 8.3x, derived from page data), boxmuller_sse2 3.752 ns (about 5.0x, derived from page data), ziggurat 6.731 ns (about 2.8x, derived from page data). normaldist (double): cpp11random 32.245 ns vs ziggurat 7.086 ns (4.55x as listed in the README).
compiler_and_flags: clang 6.1 on macOS 64-bit (from the result file name Corei5-3330S@2.70GHz_mac64_clang6.1 linked in the README); build/premake4.lua uses Optimize with -mavx -Wall -Wextra -std=c++11
tradeoffs: Bulk fill API (normaldistf(float*, n)); the SSE2/AVX variants need 16/32-byte aligned buffers and n multiples of 2/8/16/32, depend on sse_mathfun/avx_mathfun approximations of log and sin/cos, and Box-Muller needs n even. Ziggurat is Jochen Voss's implementation. The results list SIMD variants only for single precision.
caveats: Not a like-for-like comparison: cpp11random pays for std::minstd_rand plus the library's normal_distribution (which itself discards values), while the other implementations use a bare LCG, so part of the gap is the cheaper uniform source. The CLT variants fail the repo's own kurtosis check. Single 2012-era CPU and a 2015 toolchain. Compiler version and flags were inferred from a result file name and the premake script rather than the README text, so the tier could be argued as B.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github ziggurat SIMD normal random numbers C++ faster than std::normal_distribution AVX2'; opened the repo page, readme.md, build/premake4.lua and commits page.

name: SIMD-MT (SIMD-friendly Mersenne Twister engines)
baseline: std::mt19937 (also uniform_real_distribution, POSIX random, lrand48, drand48 and the author's scalar reference MT)
workload: Google Benchmark per-call time of IRNG (integer) and FRNG (float) generators built from 8 interleaved Mersenne Twister streams vs std::mt19937 and others.
claimed_speedup: README (Travis CI run): BM_IRNG_next 2.32 ns and BM_FRNG_next 2.31 ns vs BM_mt19937 6.33 ns (about 2.7x, derived from page data) and BM_uniform_real_distribution 6.84 ns; the author's scalar reference MT takes 3.45 ns.
hardware: Travis CI VM, 2 x 2800.17 MHz CPUs, L3 33792 KiB (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only. It is not the std::mt19937 sequence: it runs NumberOfStreams=8 Mersenne Twister states (alignment 64) and relies on compiler auto-vectorization; no analysis of inter-stream seeding or correlation is given.
caveats: First-party numbers from a shared CI VM with no compiler or flags stated; the author notes the edge over his reference is smaller on his laptop ('your mileage may vary'). 2020 code with no later activity.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/mersenne-twister?l=c%2B%2B (SIMD-MT listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: simdrng (SIMD Xoshiro256++, ChaCha and Philox generators)
workload: Google Benchmark on CI: u64 buffer fill of 4096 values and single-value calls for scalar vs xsimd-dispatched generators, double generation via uniform() vs std::uniform_real_distribution, and std::mt19937_64 single-value calls.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark JSON (gcc-15): XoshiroSIMD fill_u64 1645 ns per 4096 values (about 2.49e9 values/s) vs scalar Xoshiro fill_u64 3835 ns (about 1.07e9 values/s), about 2.3x (derived from page data); scalar Xoshiro uniform() 1.32 ns vs std::uniform_real_distribution 4.65 ns (about 3.5x, derived from page data); std::mt19937_64 single u64 call 1.60 ns. docs/benchmarks.rst: 'Xoshiro reaches ~2.3x its scalar loop' in bulk fill and uniform() 'roughly 3x' faster than std::uniform_real_distribution.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-15 (also gcc-14, clang-19, clang-20 result directories); CMake Release with the 'bench' preset (-march=x86-64-v3) and xsimd runtime dispatch
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (cpu_model.txt; GitHub-hosted runner, Google Benchmark reports 4 CPUs at 2445 MHz)
tradeoffs: C++20, needs xsimd and poet (single-header branch available); each SIMD generator keeps a 256-value (2 KiB for u64) output buffer, so state is larger and single-value calls are slower than scalar xoshiro. Python bindings (nanobind, numpy.random.Generator compatible) included. Philox and ChaCha variants are scalar, SIMD-dispatch and -march=native builds.
caveats: The gain is for bulk fills only: single-value SIMD calls cost 2.82 ns vs 0.94 ns for scalar Xoshiro, so a one-value-at-a-time loop is slower than the baseline. The mt19937_64 figure is a per-call time, not a bulk-fill figure, so it is not directly comparable to the fill numbers. Numbers come from a shared CI runner. License is BSD-3-Clause with an added acknowledgement clause (clause 4); that SPDX id is not on the OSI-approved list as far as I know, so usability is marked reference although the text is permissive; the orchestrator may want to reclassify. Comparison against std::mt19937_64 in bulk was not measured.
found_via: GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/random-number-generation?l=c%2B%2B and github.com/topics/philox; opened the repo page, readme.md, docs/benchmarks.rst, CMakePresets.json, the benchmark-results branch (JSON, cpu_model.txt) and the commits page.

name: seiran (seiran128 PRNG)
workload: 64-bit values generated per ns using the xoshiro/xoroshiro speed harness (harness.c), compared against ten other 64-bit generators.
claimed_speedup: README table (64-bit values/ns): seiran128 1.20 vs xoshiro256** 0.99, xoroshiro128+ 1.13, pcg64_xsh_rr 0.38, mt19937_64 0.32, sfc64 1.21; README: 'about 3.7 times faster than Mersenne Twister (64-bit version)' (1.20/0.32, derived 3.75x).
tradeoffs: Two-word (128-bit) LFSR state with an add/rotate/multiply output scrambler, period 2^128-1, jump of 2^64; no 32-bit variant; not cryptographically secure (the author recovered state from three outputs with Z3). Portable, no 128-bit multiply. CC0 dedication, so no patent grant.
caveats: First-party measurement with compiler flags unstated; the speed edge over xoshiro256** is only about 1.2x and seiran128 ties sfc64 (1.21), so the headline win is over mt19937_64 and PCG64 only. The author states that, being new, it has not been investigated by others. PractRand 32 TB, BigCrush and hwd results are the author's own.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng?l=c&o=desc&s=stars (andanteyk/prng-seiran listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: ra_prng / ra_core (array-permutation PRNG)
baseline: xoshiro256** and Philox4x32-10 (also ChaCha20, /dev/urandom and MT19937 reseed cost in other benchmarks)
workload: Single-core 'real throughput' (MB/s) for reinitialize-per-call batches of K words (K=1 and K=255) and for one long stream, with init time and per-word generation time reported separately.
claimed_speedup: README (measured 2026-09-12): ra_core_singleblock K=255 20018.1 MB/s vs Xoshiro256** K=255 2937.2 MB/s and Philox4x32-10 K=255 1007.9 MB/s, which the README states as '~6.8x faster than Xoshiro256** and ~19.9x faster than Philox'. At K=1 singleblock 307.3 MB/s vs Xoshiro256** 544.8 MB/s (slower), and ra_core_orbit stream 986.6 MB/s vs Xoshiro256** stream 3171.8 MB/s (about 3.2x slower).
tradeoffs: 32-bit generator with about 2 KB of state (two 256-entry arrays that permute each other); 'singleblock' mode gives at most 255 words per key/address with no reseed, and 'orbit' mode is for long streams. Not cryptographic. Python binding via pip-ra-core. Non-commercial licence.
caveats: Weak evidence, kept for completeness. The K=255 'singleblock' row reports about 0.00 ns/word steady-state generation and 0.191 ns/word total (almost all of it init time), which looks implausible for a data-dependent permutation loop and may be a benchmark artefact; the README itself documents an earlier benchmark fairness bug (inlining) and an earlier 30303 MB/s claim that was not reproducible. The comparison is for a different usage pattern (255 words per key, reinit-per-call) than streaming, where ra_core loses to xoshiro256**. License CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is non-OSI and non-commercial. The CSAI2025 paper was accepted but, per the README, never presented or published. First-party and single machine.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng?l=c&o=desc&s=stars (ooalahhq/ra_prng listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: cpp-random-benchmarks (PCG and xoshiro vs std::mt19937 shootout)
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, ranlux24/48, knuth_b and rand())
workload: Mean time per generated number (Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions) for xoshiro, pcg-cpp, wjakob pcg32, Jenkins small PRNG, rand() and the std engines.
claimed_speedup: README table: xoshiro256++ 1.06 ns (946.7M/s) and pcg32_fast 0.933 ns (1071.97M/s) vs std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns (294.3M/s) and std::mt19937 3.70 ns (270.7M/s), about 3.2x and 4.0x (derived from page data); pcg32 1.09 ns, pcg64_fast 1.31 ns, pcg64 1.98 ns, std::ranlux48 98.3 ns, rand() 15.4 ns.
tradeoffs: A benchmark harness, not a library; CMake downloads the engines from their own repos. Winners are projects already catalogued (imneme/pcg-cpp, prng.di.unimi.it xoshiro, wjakob/pcg32).
caveats: Reported as third-party Tier A evidence for already-known projects (pcg-cpp, xoshiro, wjakob pcg32). Builds without -march=native, so the AVX pcg32_8 variant was not measured; standard library behind the clang build is not stated; 2012-era CPU. AGPL-3.0 applies to the harness.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD random number generator faster than xoshiro PCG benchmark github' (zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks listed); opened the repo page (README.adoc text) and commits page.

name: libchaos (KISS, Xoroshiro128Plus, Xorshf96 and other PRNGs)
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, ranlux24/48, knuth_b)
workload: Google Benchmark items/s for 'Next' calls of libchaos PRNGs vs STL engines, run on Travis CI.
claimed_speedup: README: CHAOS_PRNG_XOROSHIRO128PLUS 178.426M items/s, CHAOS_PRNG_XORSHF96 185.148M, CHAOS_PRNG_ABYSSINIAN 165.754M, CHAOS_PRNG_KISS 99.9175M vs STL mt19937 68.239M and mt19937_64 60.0674M items/s (Xoroshiro128Plus about 2.6x mt19937, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.7 or newer required; flags not stated
tradeoffs: Library built around 'chaos machines' (hashes and PRNGs) with its own push/pull API; the PRNG classes are listed with seed, output and period; whether they satisfy the C++ UniformRandomBitGenerator interface was not checked. Several generators (Xoroshiro128+, KISS, Xorshf96) are ports of existing algorithms.
caveats: 2016-2017 numbers measured on a shared Travis VM with no stated compiler flags or CPU; the libchaos xoroshiro128+ code was not inspected, and the speed edge is essentially what any xorshift-family generator gives over MT19937. The benchmark source tests/b_generators.cc was not opened. Most of the library is not about speed.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/random?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars; opened the repo page, README.md, LICENSE and commits page.

name: benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD (AVX Philox4x32-10)
baseline: xoshiro256**, PCG64 and std::mt19937 (also an at::mt19937 implementation shipped in the repo)
workload: Wall time in seconds to generate 134,217,728 random numbers with 1 to 1024 threads (and 8 to 8.6e9 numbers on 1 thread), global vs thread-local generators.
claimed_speedup: results/README.md, 1 thread, 134217728 numbers (best average): philox_simd (global) 0.176 s and philox_simd (thread local) 0.188 s vs xoshiro256** 0.651 s, pcg64 0.659 s, std::mt19937 1.609 s, at::mt19937 0.393 s, scalar philox 0.439 s; about 3.7x vs xoshiro256** and pcg64 and 9.1x vs std::mt19937 (derived from page data).
hardware: 16 x Intel Xeon E5-1660 v4 @ 3.20 GHz (1 socket), Ubuntu 18.04, turbo boost off, performance governor
tradeoffs: x86-only SIMD (x86intrin.h, built with -march=native); a counter-based Philox generator, so streams and statistical properties differ from xoshiro/PCG/MT; PhiloxSIMD.h has an UNSHUFFLE switch to match the non-SIMD output order. The repo is a benchmark harness with the headers inside, not a packaged library.
caveats: No LICENSE file found in the repo (LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt and COPYING all absent), so usability is reference; the 'at' namespace suggests the Philox code was taken from PyTorch ATen, which was not verified. At tiny counts (8 numbers) xoshiro256** is faster (1.58e-7 s vs 1.79e-7 s for philox_simd global). 2019 results on GCC 7.4.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/philox (syed-ahmed/benchmark-rngs listed); opened the repo page, README.md, results/README.md, CMakeLists.txt, PhiloxSIMD.h and commits page.
